title: Asking the engine what it meant
subtitle: One input's convention was ambiguous in the vendor's documentation, and guessing wrong would silently extract the wrong token; so at startup the runtime runs a tiny batch both ways and refuses to start unless exactly one answer is consistent

stats.label: tokens spent at startup to settle the question
runs of the same micro-batch, one per convention

lede: The mining engine takes an input that tells it which token's hidden state to gather for each sequence. The vendor's documentation leaves its convention open. Those hidden states feed a corpus of hundreds of millions of vectors that my research clusters and measures. The silent kind of error, which the detector in A detector for a silent corruption exists to catch after the fact, is the kind worth refusing to risk at all. So the runtime asks the engine, during warm-up. The output is decoded in software for the checksum, so no assumption about the output format leaks into the test.
quote: A systematic off-by-one would corrupt every vector in the same way, and the corruption would look like a slightly different model rather than a bug.
evidence: Defensive integration with vendor runtimes: a startup self-test that runs a 3-token micro-batch under both readings of an ambiguous engine input and refuses to start unless exactly one is consistent.
Data integrity for embedding corpora: hundreds of millions of hidden-state vectors guarded against a systematic off-by-one that would look like a different model rather than a bug.
Numerical verification: checksums over the first 64 output values per sequence, decoded in software, with the proven convention frozen for the life of the process.
author: Corey James
